items.title: Dippin' Dots Wasn't Supposed To Be Ice Cream...
items.description:
If you were a child of the 1990's then you probably had a soft spot for Dippin' Dots. Known as "the ice cream of the future," the frozen dessert became ubiquitous at stadiums, theme parks and zoos. But despite their popularity, few realize that the science behind those tiny frozen beads was originally developed to create cattle feed. 

In this episode of Weird History Food, we’re diving into the surprising story and science behind Dippin’ Dots to find out how they're made, what makes them differ
items.why_watch: The origin story here is genuinely surprising: the flash-freezing technology behind Dippin' Dots was invented for agricultural use, not dessert. Weird History Food traces how a cattle-feed experiment ended up in theme park freezers across America. It's a tidy 14 minutes of food history with a satisfying 'how did that happen?' arc.

items.title: Why Study Classics?
items.description:
Why do we study Classics?

Studying classics, or the literature, history, and culture of ancient Greece and Rome, is important for a number of reasons. By studying classics, we can gain a deeper understanding of the history and development of Western civilization and the ways in which it has influenced the world we live in today.

First and foremost, classics provide us with a rich and diverse cultural heritage. The ancient Greeks and Romans have left a lasting legacy on Western civilization, an
items.why_watch: At just three minutes, this is less a lecture and more a compact case for why ancient Greek and Roman culture still shapes the way we argue, govern, and tell stories. It won't convert a skeptic, but it's a useful articulation of the 'so what' question that Classics students get asked at every dinner party.

fern_data.greeting: The sky right now is that specific late-summer amber — not golden, just tired and warm, the colour of old varnish. Which makes it exactly the right hour to learn that Dippin' Dots was a livestock feed experiment before it was a fairground staple, and that preserved human brains have been turning up by the thousands, stubbornly intact, for reasons scientists are only now starting to untangle.
